steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on making audio-visual synchronization models lightweight by distilling a large multimodal Transformer model (VocaLiST) into a small one. Motivate why small models matter, review the existing sync models, and summarize our method and results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- What audio-visual synchronization is and why it matters downstream
- Need for small, fast models on mobile devices
- Existing approaches: two-stream similarity models, then Transformer-based SOTA
- Problem: SOTA models too big for edge devices
- Our proposal (MTDVocaLiST) and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Task definition
  - decide whether mouth movements and speech in a video are in sync
  - out-of-sync video -> errors in downstream tasks: audio-visual user authentication, dubbing, lip reading, active speaker detection, audio-visual source separation
  - sync model = indispensable front-end for these tasks
- Why lightweight
  - downstream tasks often run on mobile devices; need small size + fast inference
  - user experience examples: fixing sync error in user-generated phone videos; audio-visual authentication in finance mobile apps
  - so lightweight sync model worth exploring
- Existing approaches
  - typical framework: estimate similarity between audio and visual segments
  - SyncNet: two-stream architecture; maximize similarity of in-sync features, minimize for out-of-sync
  - Perfect Match (PM): relative similarities between multiple audio features and one visual feature; multi-way matching objective
  - AVST (Audio-Visual Synchronisation with Transformers) and VocaLiST: current SOTA; Transformers learn multimodal interaction, classify directly whether a pair is synced; excellent performance
- Problem
  - AVST and VocaLiST: large memory, high compute -> unsuitable for edge devices
- Our work
  - MTDVocaLiST: small version of VocaLiST distilled by mimicking its multimodal Transformer behavior
  - uncertainty weighting: assess varying significance of Transformer behavior across layers -> enhanced model
  - first attempt (to our knowledge) to distill by mimicking multimodal Transformer behavior for an audio-visual task
  - beats similar-size SOTA SyncNet and PM by 15.65% and 3.35%
  - reduces VocaLiST size by 83.52%, performance still comparable

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

The audio-visual synchronization task is about deciding whether the mouth movements and the speech in a video are in sync or not. If a video is out of sync, it can cause errors in a lot of tasks, for example audio-visual user authentication, dubbing, lip reading, active speaker detection, and audio-visual source separation. So an audio-visual synchronization model is often an indispensable front-end model for these downstream tasks. Many of these downstream tasks run on mobile devices, and they need small models and fast inference. Small model size and fast inference are needed for a good user experience, for example when correcting the synchronization error of videos that users record on mobile phones, or when doing audio-visual user authentication in finance mobile applications. For these applications, it is worth exploring a lightweight audio-visual synchronization model.

A typical framework for audio-visual synchronization is to estimate the similarity between audio segments and visual segments. SyncNet introduced a two-stream architecture for estimating the cross-modal feature similarities. It is trained so that the similarities between features of in-sync audio-visual segments are maximized and the similarities between features of out-of-sync segments are minimized. Perfect Match (PM) instead optimizes the relative similarities between multiple audio features and one visual feature, using a multi-way matching objective function. The current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models are Audio-Visual Synchronisation with Transformers (AVST) and VocaLiST. They use Transformers to learn the multi-modal interaction and directly classify if an audio-visual pair is synchronized or not, and they get excellent performance. But both AVST and VocaLiST need a lot of memory and high computing cost, so these models are not suitable for computation on edge devices.

- Our work
  - MTDVocaLiST: small VocaLiST distilled by mimicking its multimodal Transformer behavior
  - uncertainty weighting -> varying significance of Transformer behavior across layers -> enhanced model
  - first attempt to distill via multimodal Transformer behavior for audio-visual task
  - beats SyncNet and PM by 15.65% and 3.35%; 83.52% smaller than VocaLiST, comparable performance

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

The audio-visual synchronization task is about deciding whether the mouth movements and the speech in a video are in sync or not. If a video is out of sync, it can cause errors in a lot of tasks, for example audio-visual user authentication, dubbing, lip reading, active speaker detection, and audio-visual source separation. So an audio-visual synchronization model is often an indispensable front-end model for these downstream tasks. Many of these downstream tasks run on mobile devices, and they need small models and fast inference. Small model size and fast inference are needed for a good user experience, for example when correcting the synchronization error of videos that users record on mobile phones, or when doing audio-visual user authentication in finance mobile applications. For these applications, it is worth exploring a lightweight audio-visual synchronization model.

A typical framework for audio-visual synchronization is to estimate the similarity between audio segments and visual segments. SyncNet introduced a two-stream architecture for estimating the cross-modal feature similarities. It is trained so that the similarities between features of in-sync audio-visual segments are maximized and the similarities between features of out-of-sync segments are minimized. Perfect Match (PM) instead optimizes the relative similarities between multiple audio features and one visual feature, using a multi-way matching objective function. The current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models are Audio-Visual Synchronisation with Transformers (AVST) and VocaLiST. They use Transformers to learn the multi-modal interaction and directly classify if an audio-visual pair is synchronized or not, and they get excellent performance. But both AVST and VocaLiST need a lot of memory and high computing cost, so these models are not suitable for computation on edge devices.

In this paper, we propose to distill a small version of VocaLiST, called MTDVocaLiST, by making it mimic the multimodal Transformer behavior of VocaLiST. We also propose to use uncertainty weighting, which lets us assess how important the Transformer behavior is in different layers, and this gives an enhanced MTDVocaLiST model. As far as we know, this is the first attempt to distill a model by mimicking multimodal Transformer behavior for an audio-visual task. Our model outperforms the similar-size state-of-the-art models SyncNet and PM by 15.65% and 3.35%. MTDVocaLiST reduces the size of VocaLiST by 83.52%, and its performance is still competitive and comparable to VocaLiST.

So an audio-visual synchronization model is often an indispensable front-end model for these downstream tasks. Many of these downstream tasks run on mobile devices, and they need small models and fast inference. Small model size and fast inference are needed for a good user experience, for example when correcting the synchronization error of videos that users record on mobile phones, or when doing audio-visual user authentication in finance mobile applications [1]. For these applications, it is worth exploring a lightweight audio-visual synchronization model.

It is trained so that the similarities between features of in-sync audio-visual segments are maximized and the similarities between features of out-of-sync segments are minimized. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

The audio-visual synchronization task is to determine whether the mouth movements and speech in a video are synchronized. An out-of-sync video may cause errors in many tasks, such as audio-visual user authentication [1], dubbing [2], lip reading [3], active speaker detection [4,5], and audio-visual source separation [6,7,8,9]. An audio-visual synchronization model therefore often acts as an indispensable front-end model for these downstream tasks. Such downstream tasks often run on mobile devices and require small model sizes and fast inference speed, which are needed to ensure user experience, for example when correcting the synchronization error of user-generated videos on mobile phones or performing audio-visual user authentication on finance mobile applications [1]. To work with these applications, a lightweight audio-visual synchronization model is worth exploring.

A typical framework for audio-visual synchronization tasks is to estimate the similarity between audio and visual segments. SyncNet [10] introduced a two-stream architecture to estimate cross-modal feature similarities, trained to maximize the similarities between features of in-sync audio-visual segments and minimize those of out-of-sync segments. Perfect Match (PM) [3,11] optimizes the relative similarities between multiple audio features and one visual feature with a multi-way matching objective function. Audio-Visual Synchronisation with Transformers (AVST) [12] and VocaLiST [13], the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models, incorporate Transformers [14] to learn the multi-modal interaction and directly classify whether a given audio-visual pair is synchronized, resulting in excellent performance. However, both AVST and VocaLiST require large memory and high computing costs, which makes them unsuitable for edge-device computation.

In this paper, we propose to distill a small-size version of VocaLiST, namely MTDVocaLiST, by mimicking the multimodal Transformer behavior of VocaLiST. We further propose to employ uncertainty weighting, which allows us to assess the varying significance of Transformer behavior across different layers and results in an enhanced MTDVocaLiST model. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to distill a model by mimicking multimodal Transformer behavior for an audio-visual task. Our model outperforms the similar-size state-of-the-art models SyncNet and PM by 15.65% and 3.35%. MTDVocaLiST reduces VocaLiST's size by 83.52% while still maintaining performance comparable to that of VocaLiST.
